questions.title: P, Q, S and line current
questions.prompt:
**20 marks**

A balanced three-phase workshop load is connected to **415 V, 50 Hz** and takes **25 A** at a lagging power factor of **0.86**.

a) Define:
i. real power;
ii. reactive power;
iii. apparent power;
iv. power factor. **(4)**

b) Calculate the apparent power in kVA. **(2)**

c) Calculate the real power in kW. **(2)**

d) Calculate the reactive power in kVAr. **(3)**

e) The same real power is later supplied at a corrected power factor of 0.95. Calculate the new line current. **(3)**

f) State three engineering benefits of reducing the line current for the same real power. **(3)**

g) Explain why kW, kVA and kVAr must not be treated as interchangeable units. **(3)**
questions.answer:
**a)** Standards-based/exam meanings:
- **Real power P:** average power converted to useful work/heat in the load; kW. **1**
- **Reactive power Q:** oscillating power associated with energy exchange in reactive fields; kVAr. **1**
- **Apparent power S:** RMS voltage-current product representing total VA demand; kVA. **1**
- **Power factor:** ratio `P/S`, also `cos phi` for sinusoidal conditions. **1**

**b)**
`S = sqrt(3) x 415 x 25 /1000 = 17.97 kVA`. **2**

**c)**
`P = S x pf = 17.97 x 0.86 = 15.45 kW`. **2**

**d)**
`Q = sqrt(S^2 - P^2)`
`= sqrt(17.97^2 - 15.45^2)`
`= 9.17 kVAr`. **3**

**e)** Real power remains `15.45 kW`.

`I = P/(sqrt(3) VL pf)`
`=15454/(1.732 x 415 x 0.95)`
`=22.64 A` approximately. **3**

**f)** Any three:
- lower conductor `I^2R` losses;
- lower voltage drop;
- releases feeder/transformer/switchgear current capacity;
- can reduce required current rating for future equivalent load;
- reduces heating. **3**

**g)** kW is real power, kVAr is reactive power, and kVA is vector/resultant apparent power. They describe different components of the power triangle and cannot be added arithmetically as if they were the same quantity. **3**

questions.title: MCCB ratings, fault level and selectivity
questions.prompt:
**20 marks**

A three-phase feeder has:

- design current `Ib = 178 A`
- corrected cable capacity `Iz = 220 A`
- prospective short-circuit current at the board = **18 kA**

Three candidate MCCBs are offered:

| Device | Rated/setting arrangement | Icu | Ics | Icw |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| A | 200 A fixed | 15 kA | 15 kA | not stated |
| B | 250 A frame, `Ir` adjustable; set to 200 A | 25 kA | 18 kA | 10 kA for 1 s |
| C | 250 A fixed | 36 kA | 27 kA | 20 kA for 1 s |

A downstream 63 A device has manufacturer-verified selectivity with Device B up to **8 kA**.

a) State what `In/frame rating` and `Ir` mean in an adjustable MCCB context. **(3)**

b) Define the practical meaning of `Icu`, `Ics` and `Icw`. **(6)**

c) Reject Device A, giving the key reason. **(2)**

d) Reject Device C for the stated cable/load arrangement, giving the key overload-coordination reason. **(2)**

e) Explain why Device B is the most suitable of the three on the data provided. **(3)**

f) At a downstream point the prospective fault current is 6.5 kA. What can be said about the stated selectivity between the downstream 63 A device and Device B? **(2)**

g) If the downstream prospective fault current later rises to 10 kA after a supply upgrade, what must be done? **(2)**
questions.answer:
**a)**
- frame/rated family identifies the physical breaker frame/rating envelope; **1**
- `Ir` is the adjustable long-time/overload pickup setting where provided; **1**
- the actual protection setting must be coordinated with design current and conductor capacity, not inferred from frame size alone. **1**

**b)**
- `Icu`: ultimate short-circuit breaking capacity at stated voltage/conditions; ability to interrupt the specified severe short-circuit duty. **2**
- `Ics`: service short-circuit breaking capacity; specified fault-interruption performance associated with continued service requirements under the product standard. **2**
- `Icw`: short-time withstand current for a stated duration; relevant when intentional delay/coordination makes equipment carry fault current before clearing. **2**

**c)** Device A has `Icu = 15 kA`, less than the stated prospective fault current of 18 kA. Its fault-breaking capability is insufficient on the supplied data. **2**

**d)** Device C is fixed at 250 A while the cable's corrected capacity is 220 A. With no lower overload setting provided, `In <= Iz` is not satisfied. **2**

**e)** Device B can be set to 200 A:
- `178 <= 200 <= 220`;
- `Icu 25 kA > 18 kA`;
- `Ics 18 kA` is stated;

questions.answer:
**a) Power circuit — 5 marks**

A complete sequence should show:

`L1/L2/L3 -> isolating means -> suitable short-circuit protective device -> main contactor poles -> overload current-sensing path -> motor U/V/W`

Award:
- three-phase supply/isolation — **1**
- suitable SCPD — **1**
- three main contactor poles — **1**
- overload element/current path — **1**
- motor correctly fed from three phases — **1**

**b) Control circuit — 6 marks**

Conceptual series path:

`control supply -> Stop NC -> overload auxiliary NC -> [Start NO in parallel with auxiliary holding NO] -> contactor coil -> return`

Award:
- control supply/return — **1**
- Stop NC in series — **1**
- overload NC in series — **1**
- Start NO — **1**
- holding auxiliary NO correctly parallel to Start — **1**
- contactor coil correctly placed — **1**

**c) Start/release sequence — 3 marks**

- pressing Start completes the coil circuit; **1**
- the contactor closes its main contacts and the auxiliary holding contact; **1**
- when Start is released, the holding contact maintains coil current until Stop, overload, loss of supply or another control condition opens the circuit. **1**

**d) Overload trip — 2 marks**

- overload protective function operates after its applicable time/current condition; **1**
- its NC auxiliary control contact opens, de-energizing the contactor coil so the main contacts open and disconnect the motor. **1**

- short-circuit protection must interrupt high fault current safely within its rating/coordination; **1**
- overload protection responds to sustained excessive motor current/thermal loading according to the motor/protection setting and characteristic. **1**

**f) No automatic restart — 2 marks**

b) Distinguish an RCCB from an RCBO. **(4)**

d) Compare the result with the supplied table value and state the conclusion for this comparison. **(3)**

f) State three reasons why this one `Zs` comparison does **not** by itself prove the entire installation safe. **(3)**

The protective device must operate within the required conditions/time so that the dangerous fault condition is disconnected. **(4)**

questions.title: Current Kenyan installation-law/standards framework
questions.prompt:
**20 marks**

The Kenya National Building Code 2024 lists several documents relevant to building electrical installation.

a) State the significance of the **Energy Act 2019** to electrical installation work. **(4)**
b) State the significance of **KS 662**. **(4)**
c) State the significance of **KS 1587**. **(3)**
d) Explain why the Code references the **KS IEC 60947** family. **(3)**
e) Explain why a distribution board/consumer unit assembly must also be considered against the applicable **KS IEC 61439** assembly requirements. **(3)**
f) Explain why compliance with a standard does not eliminate the need for competent design, installation, inspection and testing. **(3)**
questions.answer:
**a)**
The Energy Act provides the statutory framework for the energy/electricity sector, including authorization/licensing and obligations relating to electrical installation work and supply. Electrical work cannot be treated as purely private workmanship outside that legal framework. **(4)**

**b)**
KS 662 is the Kenyan electrical-installation requirements series referenced directly by the Building Code. It provides technical installation requirements and is therefore a primary Kenyan standards reference for building electrical work. **(4)**

**c)**
KS 1587 is the National electrical safety code referenced by the Building Code, supporting the safety framework for electrical installations. **(3)**

**d)**
The KS IEC 60947 series deals with families of low-voltage switchgear/controlgear such as circuit breakers, switches/disconnectors, contactors/starters and control devices. Referencing the family ensures the selected devices themselves meet the applicable product requirements rather than being judged only by nominal ampere rating. **(3)**

**e)**
A consumer unit/distribution assembly is more than a collection of individually rated devices. Assembly construction, ratings, compatibility, temperature, fault withstand and verified configuration matter; the applicable KS IEC 61439 requirements address low-voltage switchgear/controlgear assemblies. **(3)**

**f)**
Standards define requirements and product/installation criteria, but an actual installation still needs correct design assumptions, competent workmanship, appropriate equipment selection, inspection, measurements/tests and documented evidence. **(3)**

Referencing the family ensures the selected devices themselves meet the applicable product requirements rather than being judged only by nominal ampere rating.

A consumer unit/distribution assembly is more than a collection of individually rated devices.
